angle: Connect outsourced quality testing and the responsible distributor's remaining duties to practical OEM contract terms.

marketing.targetReader: Responsible distributors preparing a Korean cosmetics brand through a domestic OEM
marketing.readerQuestion: What quality duties remain with the brand when the manufacturer performs testing?
marketing.practicalPayoff: Check batch results, document delivery, specification changes and post-sale support before signing.
marketing.coverIntent: Question whether one quotation line saying ‘quality testing included’ is enough.
marketing.saveValue: Four document-flow checks for an OEM contract
marketing.performanceHypothesis: Test whether a contract checklist increases saves and preliminary-review inquiries.

approvedBy: Draft pending user approval — do not publish

cards.headline: Does the Factory's Quality Test Finish the Job?
body: Outsourcing testing does not remove the brand company's duties.
cards.promise: Four terms to align before signing
cards.takeaway: Outsourcing a test and managing its results are different tasks.
cards.design: Deep-navy cover with original cosmetic pump and cream-jar artwork connected to a quality record. No generic icon frame.

cards.headline: The Factory and Brand Have Different Duties

body.text: Tests raw materials, packaging and finished products, and keeps manufacturing and quality records.
Oversees the contractor and receives and manages batch-specific test results and related records.

cards.takeaway: An OEM contract does not remove the responsible distributor's quality duties.
cards.design: Two clearly separated responsibility panels. Keep manufacturing and distribution roles visually distinct.

cards.headline: The Same Product Is Not Always Tested Twice

body.text: This may apply when testing is outsourced to an eligible facility and batch-specific results exist.
Contractor oversight, receipt and retention of records, and final-product quality control still remain.

cards.takeaway: Check the outsourcing conditions and batch results—not only the test location.
cards.design: Stack the exception above the remaining duties, with stronger emphasis on the duties that continue.

cards.headline: Test Records Must Match the Product Batch
body: Does the delivered product show its batch number?
Can you identify the test result for that batch?
Who receives required product and quality records, and when?
cards.takeaway: A message saying “test complete” may not identify the products being delivered.
cards.design: Three stacked, numbered questions connect the delivered batch to test results and required records.

cards.headline: Write the Document Flow into the Contract
body: Specify which batch results must be delivered.
Set the delivery time and responsible reviewer.
Retain the records under the company's quality rules.
cards.takeaway: Agree on who reviews the results and when—not only who pays for testing.
cards.design: A four-step vertical timeline from testing through record retention, using large numbers and a thin gold rule.

cards.headline: Recheck Any Change to the Approved Specification

body.text: Identify the approved sample, product specifications, container, packaging and necessary test standards.
Require advance notice and supporting records, then confirm the change and effective date in writing.

cards.takeaway: Set the notice, approval and internal review process for specification changes.
cards.design: Stacked before-and-after panels distinguish the approved specification from change review, using document and refresh icons.

cards.headline: Which Records Must Be Shared?

body.text: Manufacturers must share manufacturing and quality records needed for quality control.
This depends on the design, development and production model, quality and safety impact, and trade-secret scope in the contract.
Calling records confidential does not automatically remove the duty to share necessary quality records.

cards.takeaway: Distinguish quality records to share from technical information to protect.
cards.design: Three full-width ruled sections with 21px body type. Shorter title and plain verbs preserve the duty, all three exception factors and the confidentiality boundary.

cards.headline: A Contract Cannot Transfer Statutory Duties.
cards.takeaway: Separate commercial liability from duties imposed by cosmetics law.
cards.design: Cream typography-only interlude with one short divider and generous negative space.

cards.headline: Four Terms to Align Before an OEM Contract
body: Approved sample and product, container and packaging specifications
Testing party and the legal conditions for outsourced testing
Delivery timing for batch results and required records
Owners for changes, nonconforming results and post-sale record support
cards.takeaway: Compare the quotation, contract and quality rules side by side.
cards.design: A saved-reference checklist with four document rows and restrained numbering.

cards.headline: Align All Three Documents Before Signing

body.text: The manufacturer's quotation or draft contract, test-certificate guidance, and any current quality rules you have.
Who tests, how batch results are delivered, whether the contract and quality rules name matching owners, and what remains to be agreed.

cards.takeaway: Request a free preliminary document review from ETHOS Administrative Attorney Office.
cards.design: Stacked light and navy panels separate source materials from the preliminary review. No button, contact details or QR code.
